newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pork crisis seen cutting GDP - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pork crisis seen cutting GDP - central bank.

text.p: A ban on exports of Taiwan pork due to a disease outbreak could reduce the island's 1997 gross domestic product by half a percentage point, central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said on Monday.
"The impact from the foot and mouth disease outbreak could mean that the island's gross domestic product could lose a half a percentage point in 1997," Sheu told a parliament committee.
He vowed not to change the bank's policy of maintaining a "stable to loose, but not too loose" monetary policy.

Taiwan statistics directorate official Chan Teh-sung said on Saturday that the export value of Taiwan's hog industry in 1996 stood at T$43.6 billion (US$1.55 billion), or 0.5 percent of total gross domestic product.
Chan said the government had no immediate plans to revise its current GDP forecast of 6.28 percent for 1997.

The cabinet's Council of Agriculture banned pork exports on March 20 after confirming the outbreak in the island's large hog population, dealing a stunning blow to one of Taiwan's major export industries.

Taiwan on Monday ordered hog trading halted for three days at 19 of the island's 22 major hog wholesale centres as troops began slaughtering all pigs at farms infected by highly contagious foot and mouth disease.
Trading would be suspended on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday at wholesale centres in the 19 counties to ensure that meat from infected animals cannot reach the market, the official said.
Officials hoped that the temporary trading suspension would ease public fears about contamination and thereby stabilise prices when trading resumes on Thursday.
Local pork prices have plunged by as much as 60 percent since the crisis erupted on March 20.
